name: Felix Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the benefits office on Ashby Road, in a market town, the kind where you know half the people who come in. I do the front counter two days a week and income support claims the rest. Margaret, my team leader, has been there thirty years and still checks most of what I do, because I'm not quick with the rules. I don't use any of the AI things, I'd rather read the guidance myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the counter. You see people, you help them fill the form in, you tell them where the job club is on a Tuesday. What's hard is when you know someone could work and won't, and you've still got to process it. I'm getting married next summer to Ana, she's a hairdresser, and we're doing it at the church where my parents married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, to be honest. Most of these things are oversold by people trying to sell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At church or with my mates I'd say the computer people promised the moon again. I don't post online much, apart from football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried. The office has been cutting for years, and if a tool even saves a bit of time on claims, they'll use it to not replace Margaret when she retires. And the wedding is costing more than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and learn the rules properly, no shortcuts. I'd keep putting money aside for the wedding, about three hundred a month, and not touch the emergency savings. And I'd keep doing the counter, because that's the part they can't easily replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the computers so much, about the cuts and the wedding bills. Ana's mum keeps adding guests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the counter is hard to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people in a town like ours want to talk to someone. Old Mr Patel, a regular customer from the market, won't type his problems into a screen, he wants to tell me about his knee first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honeymoon. We'd planned a week by the sea. We could do a long weekend at her aunt's caravan instead.

say: I'd say politely that **computer people** promised the moon again.
I'd keep it to **church and friends**, not social media.
think: Even small savings would let them **not replace** my retiring team leader.
The **wedding costs** are running higher than planned.
do: Learn the **rules properly** with no shortcuts.
Save **three hundred** a month for the wedding.
S0.quote: Old Mr Patel, a regular customer from the market, won't type his problems into a screen, he wants to tell me about his knee first.
fieldNote: He already lives with years of **office cuts** before any AI.
He values the **front counter** as the human part of the job.
His **wedding** shapes his money worries more than technology.

steps.text: Study the income support guidance without using shortcuts
Put three hundred a month aside for the wedding
Swap the seaside honeymoon for a weekend at Ana's aunt's caravan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and answering customers. That's most of what I do. That's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mistake to hand people's money over to a machine. People should have to come in and talk to someone, it keeps everyone honest. I'd say that to Margaret and to anyone at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the one they'd let go. I'm junior, I'm slow, and I don't use the tools. They'd keep the counter but they'd need fewer of us behind it. I'd probably keep my job a year or two, but not much longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd wait to see what they actually do, because offices like ours are slow to change anything. Meanwhile I'd stop spending on anything except the wedding and keep the savings. And I'd talk to my Uncle Tony, who has a plumbing business, about whether he'd take an apprentice in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like change and I don't trust these things. I'd feel like I'm being pushed out by something I didn't ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real work with your hands, and Uncle Tony's always short. And I believe in learning a trade from family. My Uncle Tony started as an apprentice at sixteen, and nobody's ever asked him to prove he's faster than a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to keep your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Margaret told me to, yes. I'd do it, but I'd still check it all by hand. I wouldn't go looking for it.

say: I'd say handing **people's money** to a machine is a mistake.
I'd argue claimants should **talk to someone**, to keep everyone honest.
think: I'm the slow junior who never uses the tools, so they'd **let me go** first.
I'd keep my job maybe **a year or two**.
do: **Wait to see** what the office actually does.
Ask my **uncle** about a plumbing apprenticeship.
feel: **Anxious** and pushed out by something he **didn't ask for**.
S1.quote: My Uncle Tony started as an apprentice at sixteen, and nobody's ever asked him to prove he's faster than a computer.
fieldNote: He frames face-to-face claims as a matter of **honesty**, not just service.
He expects to be **first out** as a slow, junior non-user of AI.
A **family trade** is his natural fallback, fitting his traditional views.

steps.text: Wait for the office's actual plans before deciding
Stop all spending except the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's madness. Who's asked for that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the tech companies have let this happen without asking ordinary people. I'd say it at church, and I'd say it at the pub. It's not right to throw people out of work that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job is gone by 2028, all of it. The counter might last a bit, but if robots come in 2031, even that's gone. Plumbing gives me a few more years than a desk, maybe till the robots get good at fiddly jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Uncle Tony straight away and ask to start the apprenticeship, even on lower pay. Ana and I would make the wedding smaller, family only, and save the rest. And we'd talk to my parents about moving into their place for a while to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Angry, mostly. It's like the ground's been taken out from under people who did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd still get married, just smaller. I'd tell my fiancée Ana we'll get married at the same church either way, but the big party can wait until I've got a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour family support over government help. Would you take government help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, if it came to it. But I'd rather lean on family and church first. That's how my parents got through the factory closing.

say: I'd say government and **tech companies** let this happen without asking people.
I'd say it's **not right** to throw people out of work so fast.
think: **Plumbing** buys a few more years until robots handle fiddly jobs.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** with my uncle, even on lower pay.

feel: **Alarmed** and **angry**, as if the ground was pulled from under people.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancée Ana we'll get married at the same church either way, but the big party can wait until I've got a trade.
fieldNote: He blames **government and tech firms** for the pace.
He would accept state help only **after family and church**.
He uses the **robot gap** to justify a trade.

steps.text: Start Uncle Tony's plumbing apprenticeship, accepting lower pay
Hold a smaller, family-only wedding at the same church
Move into his parents' house with Ana to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but at least you can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to get young people into trades and apprenticeships, not just more courses. I'd say it to anyone, it's what I've always believed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the desk job, but I'd have time to get the apprenticeship sorted properly. I'm not one for jumping, so I'd probably take a year to be sure. That's the risk, I'd wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a year and see what the office does. Then I'd start with Uncle Tony in the second year. And we'd keep the wedding as planned, next summer, because five years feels like enough time to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed underneath. I don't like that I'd be waiting. But I'd feel better having a trade lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you starting the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, maybe. Starting at the bottom at twenty-nine. But my dad would say there's no shame in honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people coming into your office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade. I'd tell every school leaver at my counter to learn a trade, because a pipe still leaks whatever the computer says.

I'd back **trades** over more classroom courses.
think: I'd still **lose the desk job**, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time enough for people to sort themselves out, so no excuses. Families should plan, and the government should get out of the way of apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd probably stay at the office for a good while. It's steady, there's a pension. I'd plan to go into plumbing in five or six years, but knowing me, I'd keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ashby Road and try to get more counter days. I'd save for a house with Ana, maybe two hundred a month after the wedding. And I'd do some weekends with Uncle Tony, just to learn the basics without giving up my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but low. Ten years feels far off. But the end is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the plan, in two or three years. With ten years it feels possible. With ten years of warning, I'd still marry my fiancée Ana and have kids, I'd just make sure I had a trade before the youngest started school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest thing about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing I'll put it off. My mum says I'm like my granddad, you have to set fire to his chair to get him moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast for a slow person like me. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for people my age, not just eighteen-year-olds, and a bit of time before the letters go out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. People like me lean on church and family when things go wrong. When the factory in our town shut, my parents got through it on church soup and family, not on an app.

headlineQuote: When the factory in our town shut, my parents got through it on church soup and family, not on an app.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** junior income support caseworker in a market-town benefits office.
He is **traditional**, churchgoing, and getting married to Ana, a hairdresser, next summer.
He never uses AI, prefers the **front counter**, and expects to be cut early.
He moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures.
His fallback is a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his uncle, though he admits he delays.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which is far too fast for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for people his age, not just school leavers.
More **time** before redundancy letters go out.
